ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Calamity Jane Synthetic CCD — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

text.paragraph: Establishing primary care for heavy daily drinking: a nonjudgmental, trauma-informed assessment, withdrawal risk and outpatient withdrawal management, thiamine, liver tests, nutrition, mood and safety, and housing, food and income. Concerns: She wants to stop drinking before it kills her, and does not want a lecture; She is afraid of the shakes if she stops, and has nowhere steady to stay; She is worried about her liver and her weight. [S]

tr.td: Establishing primary care for heavy daily drinking: a nonjudgmental, trauma-informed assessment, withdrawal risk and outpatient withdrawal management, thiamine, liver tests, nutrition, mood and safety, and housing, food and income
One-week review, seen the same day by addiction medicine: after withdrawal, a medicine for alcohol use disorder, the liver plan and recovery supports
Four-week review: naltrexone and the change to a monthly injection, liver stiffness, mood after four weeks without alcohol, and benefits
Ten-week review: recovery, mood, housing and results
Sixteen-week review after a two-day return to drinking: liver tests, PEth, elastography and the plan ahead
Same-day sick visit for a dental abscess

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: A nonjudgmental, trauma-informed assessment: AUDIT, DSM-5-TR criteria and PEth explained as part of care, person-first language, a female clinician and a chaperone offered, consent asked before each part of the examination, and her own goals and choices first
Addiction medicine consultation to confirm the diagnosis, review withdrawal and choose a medicine for alcohol use disorder

Outpatient withdrawal management at low risk (PAWSS 3, CIWA-Ar 9): a five-day gabapentin schedule, daily nurse checks with the CIWA-Ar in person or by the clinic phone, her friend as support, fluids and food; hospital care at once for a CIWA-Ar of 15 or more, a seizure, hallucinations, confusion or vomiting
Thiamine 100 mg by injection for three days, then by mouth, with folic acid, potassium and magnesium replacement

Medicine for alcohol use disorder: naltrexone 50 mg daily, with a monthly extended-release naltrexone injection if daily tablets are hard to keep; liver tests rechecked on treatment; acamprosate if naltrexone cannot be used; disulfiram not used; a wallet card explaining that naltrexone blocks opioid pain medicines
Liver: FIB-4 of 3.93, so transient elastography; liver enzymes, albumin, INR and platelets followed; hepatitis A and B vaccination; acetaminophen no more than 2 g a day

Mood and safety: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 again after two to four weeks without alcohol before deciding on depression treatment; a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, the rifle stored with her friend, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit

Recovery support and harm reduction: weekly contact with the clinic's peer recovery support specialist, her choice of mutual-help meetings (Alcoholics Anonymous, SMART Recovery or Women for Sobriety), and a plan for a return to drinking: call the peer specialist or the clinic, eat, do not drink alone or drive, keep taking any medicine for alcohol use disorder, and come back without shame

Housing, food, income and coverage: the clinic's community health worker helps with a Montana Medicaid application, SNAP benefits, a food bank, the local Human Resource Development Council's housing programs, Montana 211, and a free phone through the Lifeline program

Alcohol and women's health: why the same amount of alcohol does women more harm (higher blood alcohol, faster liver damage, a higher breast cancer risk), a pregnancy test, contraception if needed, and breast and cervical cancer screening at the preventive visit
Chewing tobacco: advice to stop and nicotine replacement offered whenever she is ready
Finish withdrawal safely at home without a seizure or delirium
Five days of gabapentin with daily nurse checks; CIWA-Ar 9 at intake, 10 at most, 2 at one week; no seizure, hallucinations or confusion
No drinking, her goal, with a medicine for alcohol use disorder
No alcohol for twelve weeks, then two days of drinking in late May, followed by three weeks without; PEth 820 to 24, then 64 after the lapse
Liver tests back to normal and a clear answer on liver scarring
AST 96 to 31 and ALT 44 to 24 U/L; liver stiffness 9.6 to 6.8 kPa; no advanced fibrosis
Regular meals and a healthier weight
Weight 50.0 to 52.6 kg (BMI 18.4 to 19.3); SNAP benefits and two meals a day on most days
A room of her own and health coverage
Medicaid approved by the four-week visit; a rented room through a housing program by the ten-week visit
PHQ-9 below 10, and reassessment once she has stopped drinking
PHQ-9 14 to 5 after ten weeks without alcohol

list.item: Independent in all activities; tremor in the mornings until she drinks; works when work is offered [S]

Alert and oriented; guarded at first, then frank and funny; mild tremor and sweating; no hallucinations or confusion; mood low and tired; PHQ-9 14 with item 9 scored 0, GAD-7 11; no thoughts of suicide or self-harm [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 1901-03-02: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care with daily nurse checks during withdrawal and close follow-up. Risk factors reviewed without detail: severe alcohol use disorder, depressive symptoms, early losses, past violence by a partner, housing instability and living alone at times. Firearm safety was discussed: she agreed to leave her rifle, unloaded, with her friend, who keeps it locked, during the first months of recovery. A written safety plan was made with her, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was written on the card she carries, since she has no phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit [S]
